source.title: Investigating Representation Universality: Case Study on Genealogical Representations
source.authors: David D. Baek; Yuxiao Li; Max Tegmark

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests representational alignment using cone probes, activation patching, and linear model stitching rather than the original sources’ measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper reports toy-network embeddings across random seeds, causal patching of genealogy-related subspaces in five LLMs, and stitching results. Cited findings from prior work are not recorded as rows. The prompt in the appendix is an example task instruction, not an instruction to an AI reviewing this paper.
record.test_reason: The study's own results bear on cross-model representational compatibility. It uses trainable linear stitching between OPT, Pythia, Mistral and LLaMA models (V4, with incompleteness bearing on V7). It shows consistent cone embeddings across seeds in toy MLPs (V3). It shows a causally relevant tree-like subspace recurring in five LLMs (V5). None of these methods match the originals' kNN alignment or unit-matching measures.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors present the cone-probe and stitching results as evidence that might support universal graph representations. They state that equivalent relative depths across models align strongly, which they call representation universality. They also conclude that the lack of ground-truth graph representations makes this hard to study. The small-scale caveats appear in the limitations sections rather than in the conclusion itself.
record.recipe_differences: Uses cone probing and causal activation patching for genealogy representations, and trainable linear model stitching evaluated by next-token loss; the paper does not establish a direct methodological match to the original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Stitching compatibility varies with relative layer depth: early-to-mid layers are reported as more compatible than later layers. Genealogy QA performance also depends on whether the listed tree facts are ordered by depth or shuffled.

fits_no_version.finding: Genealogy QA F1 is high only when tree facts are ordered by depth and drops when they are shuffled.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM in-context relational reasoning depends on fact ordering (a capability result, not representational convergence).

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Responsible Foundation Models
record.problems: The genealogy task uses a relatively small 15-node tree and models achieve near-perfect accuracy on it; the authors say generalization to larger or more complex graphs is unclear. The stitching method assumes a simple linear mapping, tests a limited set of architectures and scales, and relies on plotted results without numeric values transcribed in the text. No ground-truth representations of graphs are available.
record.rows_left_out: The PCA and full-layer patching comparisons in Figure 3 and the per-layer series in Figure 4 are not included as separate rows; the text reports their qualitative comparison (cone patching is comparable to or larger than PCA, full-layer patching is larger, and early-to-mid layers have stronger effects). These comparison conditions do not directly test cross-model feature recurrence. Figure 5’s test-loss sweep for an unspecified model pair is also omitted because the pair is not identifiable from the supplied text.

untested.parts: No test of whether alignment increases with size or capability, although the models span 410M–8B.
All of it; no vision or multimodal models are studied.
Shared features or subspaces in large networks; any quantitative seed-to-seed similarity.
Relative representations; unpaired alignment; non-linear maps; cross-family results (Mistral, LLaMA) that are described but not shown.
Identity of specific neurons, SAE features or circuits across models.
All of it; only one measure (stitching loss) and in-distribution Pile data.
Whether shared data or objectives explain alignment (the stitching models largely share Pile-like data); plateau.

missing.what: Stitching results involving Mistral-7B-Instruct and LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct (cross-tokenizer), which are stated as included but not shown in any figure.
Fig. 5 right: test loss vs. same-relative-depth cut position for an unspecified pair (declared in rows_left_out, but it is the main stitching curve).
Per-layer causal effect for Llama-3.1-8B (cone vs. PCA vs. full layer), with standard errors; effect is stronger in early-to-mid layers.

record.verdict_notes: All evidence is figure-only, with no transcribed numbers. The cone probe finds a geometric structure per model and does not match features across models, so the V5 support is weak. The stitching models cover sizes but no scale trend is analysed, so V1 stays untested. The appendix prompt is a task example; no instructions were followed.

versions.untested_parts: The study compares model representations but does not test whether alignment increases with model size or capability.
No vision-language or paired image-caption representations are studied.
Tests toy MLP embeddings on two tree structures, not shared features or subspaces in large networks.
Tests linear layer stitching, not relative representations, stitching as a general method, or alignment without paired data.
Tests recurrence of a cone-probe tree-like structure, not identity of particular neurons, SAE features, or circuits.
Does not compare similarity metrics or test sensitivity to neighbourhood settings or out-of-distribution inputs.
Reports incomplete/position-dependent stitching compatibility, but does not test whether shared training data or objectives explain alignment rather than a common model of reality.

tranche.reason: Cone probing, causal patching and trainable linear stitching provide different methods aimed at representational universality and compatibility.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v2 dated 23 November 2025. Cone-subspace recurrence is qualitative geometric evidence; stitching uses general next-token data and does not specifically establish shared genealogy representations.

statements.correction: Early-to-mid-layer representations align more closely than later-layer representations; mid-layer stitches are often compatible; later-layer stitches have higher loss; exact loss gaps and near-complete alignment are not stated.
statements.problem: The early-to-middle-layer trend is correct, but the near-completeness framing exceeds this study's qualitative evidence.
